about: The introit of the Third Sunday of Advent, from which the day takes its name of Gaudéte. The antiphon is the opening of the same Mass's epistle, and the psalm verse the opening of its offertory: one Mass says the same thing three times, each time more fully.

s01.translation: Rejoice in the Lord always; again I say, rejoice. Let your gentleness be known to all people, for the Lord is near. Be anxious about nothing, but in every prayer make your petitions known to God.

translation_citations.title: The Missal for the Laity (1846)
translation_citations.locator: parallel Ordinary and Advent propers, examined edition

s02.translation: You have blessed Your land, O Lord; You have ended Jacob's captivity.

translation_citations.title: The Missal for the Laity (1846)
translation_citations.locator: parallel Ordinary and Advent propers, examined edition

s03.translation: Glory be to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit. As it was in the beginning, is now, and ever shall be, world without end. Amen.

translation_citations.title: The Missal for the Laity (1846)
translation_citations.locator: parallel Ordinary and Advent propers, examined edition

s04.narrative: After the doxology the Introit antiphon is repeated from Gaudéte to the psalm verse — by the choir at a sung Mass, by the priest himself at a low Mass.

s05.translation: Rejoice in the Lord always; again I say, rejoice. Let your gentleness be known to all people, for the Lord is near. Be anxious about nothing, but in every prayer make your petitions known to God.

translation_citations.title: The Missal for the Laity (1846)
translation_citations.locator: parallel Ordinary and Advent propers, examined edition

w037.explanation: In the doxology the verb remains unspoken. Liturgical usage supplies the wish “glory be”.
